title: Made-to-Measure Stainless Steel Worktops: What to Check Before Ordering
excerpt: Planning a stainless steel worktop? Find out which measurements, sink positions and storage details help us prepare a useful quote for your kitchen.
cta: Planning a worktop for your kitchen?
contact: Send us approximate dimensions, photos of the space and what you need underneath. We’ll discuss the layout and prepare an initial estimate.
content:
A four-metre worktop tells us the length, but it doesn’t tell us the whole job. We still need to know where the sinks will sit, what storage you need underneath and how the unit will fit around the equipment already in place.

At Midia M Metal, we make stainless steel worktops and kitchen units to suit the space and the people using them. Here is what helps us turn an initial enquiry into an agreed design.

Start with the space and the daily work

Tell us what happens at the worktop. Preparing ingredients, washing equipment and plating food can call for different arrangements. Explain what needs to stay within reach and where people move during a busy service.

Approximate length, depth and height give us a starting point. Include photos of nearby appliances, doors and pipework. A wall that looks straight in a photograph may need checking during the site visit, so initial measurements are not the final production dimensions.

Decide where the sinks and storage belong

For a stainless steel worktop with sinks, we need to discuss the number of bowls, their position and the space you want beside them. Tell us what will be washed and show us the existing water and waste connections.

Underneath, you may want cupboards, open shelving or room for equipment. Think about door access as well as storage capacity. A cupboard is less useful if its door cannot open properly beside another unit.

  • Which side should the sink or draining area be on?
  • What needs to fit below the work surface?
  • Are there pipes or equipment that need access later?
  • Does the unit need to meet an existing worktop?

Understand what the initial price covers

We prepare an initial estimate from the measurements and requirements you give us. Preparing a quote is free. A price based on an approximate length remains an estimate until the dimensions and layout are agreed.

Two units of equal length can have different prices. Cupboards, sink arrangements, material and fabrication details all affect the work involved. A revised layout can bring the total down or increase it; we explain the final price before you commit to production.

Confirm the details before fabrication

Once the initial estimate is acceptable, we arrange the next steps. Where a site visit is needed, we check the measurements and discuss the design. Site measurement is usually free, depending on location; any charge is confirmed beforehand.

We also need to consider delivery access. Tell us about narrow doorways, stairs and equipment that cannot be moved. The agreed specification and final price come to you for approval before we start making the unit.

Plan the changeover

If this replaces an existing worktop, tell us when the kitchen can be made available. We will discuss the scope of delivery and installation and give you an estimated schedule once the job is agreed.

For an overview of the other items we can make, read our guide to bespoke metal fabrication. If price is your main question, our metalwork pricing guide explains the information behind an estimate.

title: Custom Metal Frames, Shelves and Table Legs: Getting the Fit Right
excerpt: Need a frame, shelf or table base in an unusual size? Here is what to consider when commissioning metalwork for your space and everyday use.
cta: Need a frame or shelf made to fit?
contact: Send a sketch, approximate measurements and a photo of where it will go. Tell us what it needs to support and we’ll discuss the next steps.
content:
A ready-made frame can be almost right and still be no use. The width fits, but a crossbar blocks a cupboard. A shelf fills the wall, but leaves too little room for the equipment underneath. A table base looks suitable until someone tries to sit at it.

With custom metal frames, shelves and table legs, we start with how the finished piece will be used. At Midia M Metal, we make these items to agreed dimensions for kitchens, workshops, commercial spaces and other individual projects.

Tell us what the frame needs to support

Overall dimensions are useful, but we also need to know what sits on the frame. Is it a work surface, a piece of equipment or stored stock? Does the weight stay in one place, or does the item move during use?

Give us any available equipment dimensions and weight information. We’ll discuss the construction once we understand the job. A photograph of a frame you like can explain the appearance, but it does not establish what your new frame needs to carry.

Leave room for people, equipment and access

For a table base, consider legroom and the position of chairs. For an equipment stand, show us any doors, drawers, cables or pipes that need clearance. A support in the wrong place can make maintenance awkward.

With shelving, tell us what will be stored and how it will be lifted on and off. Shelf depth and spacing need to suit those items, and the available wall or floor space needs to be checked.

  • What needs to fit beneath or between the supports?
  • Does anything open, slide out or need regular cleaning?
  • Will the piece be freestanding or fixed in position?
  • Does it need to line up with existing furniture?

Agree the fixing and finish

A frame may need to attach to a separate top or to existing metalwork. We need details of that connection before placing holes or fixing plates. If you already have the top, photos of its underside can be particularly useful.

We mainly work with stainless steel and can discuss other metals according to the use. Tell us whether the piece will be indoors or outdoors and what appearance you want. We’ll agree the material and finish as part of the job.

Think about how it reaches its position

A finished piece has to get through the building as well as fit its final location. Mention stairs, narrow passages or limited access when you enquire. If the job requires assembly or fitting on site, we can discuss that before quoting.

From rough sketch to agreed order

You can begin with a hand-drawn sketch and approximate measurements. We use those to discuss the design and initial price, then confirm the necessary details before production. Delivery and fitting depend on the size and location of the job.

If the existing frame is damaged rather than unsuitable, our guide to metal repairs explains what to send us for an assessment.

title: Choosing Castors and Replacement Legs for Your Equipment
excerpt: Replacing an equipment wheel or leg? Check the fixing, fitted height, load information and everyday use before choosing a replacement.
cta: Looking for a replacement castor or leg?
contact: Send photos of the whole unit, the fixing and any markings on the old part. Include the quantity you need so we can look at suitable options.
content:
When an equipment wheel breaks, it is tempting to order another that looks the same. The wheel might match, but the mounting plate may be different, or the replacement may leave one corner of the unit higher than the others.

At Midia M Metal, we supply replacement legs and castors and can assess whether a custom metal support or mounting piece is needed. These are the details that help us identify what will fit.

Start with the connection

Photograph how the castor or leg attaches to the equipment. A mounting plate and a threaded stem need different information. For a plate, we need its dimensions and fixing-hole positions. For a stem, thread and fitting details matter.

Include any model number, label or marking that is still readable. If you do not know the thread specification, say so rather than guessing. We can tell you what further information we need.

Measure the fitted height

The wheel diameter alone does not tell us how high the unit will sit. The bracket and mounting arrangement also contribute to the overall fitted height.

If only one castor is being replaced, show us the others. If you want to replace the whole set, tell us whether the present working height should stay the same. The same question applies to adjustable or fixed equipment legs.

Describe the load and the way the unit moves

Tell us the equipment’s weight if you have it, along with what it carries in use. A unit that is empty in a photograph may carry much more during the working day.

Also describe the floor and route: smooth indoor flooring, thresholds, uneven areas or outdoor use. Let us know how often the unit moves and whether it needs to turn in a confined space. Suitable load ratings and fitting details need to be confirmed for the chosen parts.

Do you need a brake?

Explain where the equipment needs to remain stationary and how it is normally positioned. If the existing castors have brakes, photograph those as well. We can discuss the replacement arrangement with the use of the whole unit in mind.

If you are changing fixed legs to wheels, mention that at the start. We need to assess the mounting arrangement and intended use before treating it as a straightforward replacement.

Check what the wheel is attached to

A new castor will not resolve a bent mounting plate or a damaged support. Send a wider photograph showing the surrounding metalwork, especially if the failure followed an impact.

We can look at whether a replacement metal component is needed alongside the supplied part. The condition and purpose of the assembly determine what is practical.

What to send with your enquiry

  • Photos of the complete unit and the old leg or castor.
  • A clear view of the fixing and any readable markings.
  • Approximate fitted height and wheel diameter, if relevant.
  • Available load information and a description of the floor.
  • The quantity required and your postcode.

With that information, we can discuss suitable options and explain anything else that needs checking before you order.

title: Metal Welding Repairs: When Is Repair Worth Considering?
excerpt: A broken weld or bent metal part does not always mean replacing the whole item. Here is what helps us assess a repair, alteration or replacement.
cta: Have damaged metalwork to show us?
contact: Send a close-up of the damage and a wider photo of the whole item. Tell us how it is used, what happened and where the job is.
content:
A cracked joint, loose bracket or bent leg can put an otherwise useful item out of action. Sometimes a repair makes sense. Sometimes the surrounding metal or the way the item is used means a replacement is the better option.

At Midia M Metal, we assess metalwork repairs by looking at the whole item and the job it needs to do. A photograph of a broken weld helps, but it is only the start of that conversation.

Show us more than the damaged area

Send a close-up and a wider view. We need to see where the damaged piece sits, what it connects to and how much access there is around it. Include the underside or reverse if you can photograph it safely.

Explain whether the item is a cupboard, frame, gate, shelf or another piece of equipment. Tell us if it is fixed in place or can be brought in for assessment.

Tell us how the damage happened

An impact, repeated movement and gradual wear describe different situations. Let us know if the item has become unsteady, has been altered or has already been repaired.

That information helps us understand whether simply repairing the visible damage would address the problem. We may need to discuss the connection, support or replacement of a larger section.

The condition of the surrounding metal matters

We need to consider the material and its condition around the damaged area, as well as access for the work. A clear-looking break does not, by itself, establish whether a repair is suitable.

If you know the material, tell us. If you don’t, photographs and any product information are useful starting points. We will confirm what can be offered after reviewing the job rather than promise a repair from a single picture.

Repair, alter or replace?

A repair may be worth considering when the rest of the item remains serviceable and the work can restore its intended use. An alteration may help where the original arrangement no longer suits the equipment or space.

A custom replacement part is another possibility when a component is too damaged or the original cannot be sourced. We discuss the practical options and price before proceeding.

Workshop work or a site visit?

Tell us the item’s size, whether it can be moved and your postcode. Those details help us work out how the job could be handled. We are based in London and consider site work according to location and scope.

For a commercial kitchen or other occupied premises, mention access hours and when the area can be made available. Any required site arrangements are agreed as part of the work.

Getting an estimate

Preparing a quote is free. Photos and a description may allow an initial estimate, but further assessment can be needed before the scope and price are confirmed. The estimated timing depends on the work and our workload.

For help putting the information together, see what to send with a metalwork enquiry.

title: Custom Metal Brackets and Fixings: Getting the Fit Right
excerpt: Standard brackets do not always fit. Learn which measurements and fixing details help us make a metal bracket for your equipment or installation.
cta: Need a bracket that fits your job?
contact: Send photos of both fixing surfaces, a rough sketch and the available dimensions. Explain what the bracket will support or connect.
content:
A bracket is a small part of a job, but a few millimetres in the wrong place can stop everything fitting together. The holes may miss the existing fixings, the bend may leave a gap, or the plate may obstruct another component.

We make custom metal brackets and connecting pieces at Midia M Metal for jobs where a standard fitting does not suit the arrangement. Before we make one, we need to understand both sides of the connection.

What is the bracket connecting?

Show us the equipment, frame or surface on each side. Tell us whether the bracket supports an item, keeps two parts aligned or holds a removable cover in position.

Its job affects the questions we ask about the material and construction. Include any known loads and explain whether there is movement or vibration during use. A similar-looking bracket from another item is a useful reference, but not a complete specification.

Which measurements are useful?

A simple sketch is often clearer than a long written description. Mark the overall dimensions, the fixing positions and the space available around the part. State the units and identify measurements that are approximate.

  • Plate width and length on each side.
  • Hole diameters and centre-to-centre distances, where known.
  • Distances from hole centres to the edges.
  • The gap or offset the bracket needs to span.
  • Any nearby parts that limit the available space.

If the original bracket is bent, don’t assume its current angle is correct. Photos of the mounting surfaces can help us establish the intended fit.

Leave access for assembly

A hole can line up perfectly and still be awkward to use if there is no room for a tool or nut behind it. Show us the access around the fixing points and tell us whether the bracket will be fitted before or after other equipment.

Also explain if it needs to come off regularly for cleaning or maintenance. That requirement belongs in the design conversation before production.

Material and finish

We mainly work with stainless steel and discuss other metals according to the job. Let us know whether the bracket is visible, used outdoors or exposed to water and cleaning products.

Material thickness and construction need to suit the intended use. You can provide a drawing or existing specification; where details are undecided, we will discuss them with you before agreeing the work.

One bracket or a matching set?

Tell us the quantity from the beginning. For a set, mark any left- and right-hand versions clearly. Two parts that look alike may need mirrored hole positions or a different orientation.

Once the design, measurements and price are agreed, we can give you an estimated production schedule. You can read more about what affects fabrication cost or send us the existing part for discussion.

title: Bespoke Metal Gates and Railings: Planning Your Order
excerpt: Planning a metal gate or railing? Start with the opening, access, fixing points and finish so the fabrication can be agreed around your property.
contact: Send photos of the full opening or boundary, approximate dimensions and your postcode. Tell us how the space is used and the style you have in mind.
content:
A gate has to fit the opening and work with the space around it. A railing needs to suit its position and the purpose it serves. Choosing the appearance is part of the job, but we also need to understand the site before agreeing the fabrication.

At Midia M Metal, we make bespoke metal gates and railings to an agreed design. Photos and approximate dimensions are a useful starting point for discussing what you need.

Show us the whole opening

Take a photograph far enough back to include both sides, the ground and the area immediately beyond. Close-ups of existing posts, walls and fixings are useful as well.

Tell us whether this is a replacement gate or a new installation. If there is already a gate, explain what works and what you want to change: its width, appearance, opening direction or everyday operation.

Think about how the space is used

Does the opening serve pedestrians, deliveries or larger equipment? What clear space needs to remain when the gate is open? Mention slopes, steps and nearby doors that could affect movement.

For railings, explain their position and intended purpose. Work around changes in level needs its design and site requirements agreed before fabrication. We establish the appropriate scope for the job rather than assume that a decorative reference image provides all the necessary details.

Discuss fixing points early

New metalwork has to connect to something. We need to assess the proposed posts, base or surrounding structure and agree the fixing arrangement.

If old metalwork has moved or become loose, show us that too. Replacing the visible section may not address an issue with its support. Access for installation also affects how the work is planned.

Choose an appearance that suits the job

A photo or sketch can explain the pattern and proportions you prefer. Tell us which features matter most and whether the new work should match an existing section.

Material and finish are discussed alongside the location and use. We mainly work with stainless steel and can discuss other metals for suitable jobs. We confirm what will be supplied and any finishing work included in the price.

Repairing part of an existing gate or railing

A damaged bracket, hinge connection or section may be a separate repair enquiry. Send photos of the damage and the complete assembly so we can discuss whether repair or replacement is practical.

Our metal repair guide explains the information that helps with that assessment.

Agree the job before it is made

We start with your requirements and an initial estimate. Where a visit is needed, we discuss the location and confirm any charge beforehand. The final dimensions, design, price and scope of fitting are agreed before production.

We are based in London and consider installation work according to its location and size. Include your postcode and any access restrictions when you contact us.

title: Custom Sheet Metal Boxes, Covers and Enclosures: What We Need to Know
excerpt: Need a metal cover, box or enclosure in a particular size? Plan the internal space, access and mounting details before having it fabricated.
cta: Need a metal box or cover made to fit?
contact: Send the size of what it needs to contain or cover, photos of its surroundings and a rough sketch. Tell us how it will be fitted and opened.
content:
A standard metal box may be the right width but too shallow. A cover may fit the equipment but block the access needed to service it. These are common reasons to have a sheet metal item made around the job.

At Midia M Metal, we make bespoke boxes, covers, panels and enclosures from agreed measurements and requirements. The first question is what the piece needs to contain, cover or protect.

Internal size and external size are different

Tell us whether your measurements describe the available space or the object that needs to fit inside. That distinction matters when there are folded edges, joints, mounting points or a removable lid.

Photos of the item and surrounding area help us understand the clearances. If you have a drawing, label the dimensions and identify any that are approximate.

Plan how it opens

Will the cover stay in place most of the time, or be removed daily? Does it need a lift-off lid, removable panel or another agreed access arrangement?

Think about the direction it opens and where the removed section can be placed. A lid needs space above it, while a front panel needs access to its fixings. Tell us which parts of the equipment must remain reachable.

Mark openings and connections

If the design needs holes or cut-outs, provide their positions and purpose. Show us any pipes, cables or existing connections that pass through or around the enclosure.

When a cover forms part of equipment with specific operating requirements, provide those specifications. A fabricated cover should not be assumed to provide a particular weather, electrical or protective rating simply because it fits. The required performance needs to be established for the job.

Agree material, edges and finish

We mainly work with stainless steel and discuss other materials where suitable. Explain the environment, cleaning routine and appearance you want.

Let us know which edges will be handled and which surfaces remain visible. These details help define the fabrication and finish rather than leaving important decisions until after the item has been made.

Replacing an existing panel or cover

If the old part is available, photograph both sides and its fixings. It can help establish the shape and mounting points. If it is bent, we also need to understand the original fit.

For a missing part, show us the opening and any matching pieces. Our guide to custom replacement metal parts explains how to start without a complete original.

From enquiry to production

Send your approximate measurements, quantity and postcode for an initial discussion. Preparing a quote is free. Once the dimensions, access details, material and price are agreed, we can confirm the estimated production timing.

A small amount of planning around fit and access makes the finished piece much easier to use. If you are unsure which details matter, start with photographs and explain the problem you need to solve.

title: What Affects the Cost of Bespoke Metalwork?
excerpt: Size is only part of a metalwork quote. Learn how material, construction, finish, quantity and installation affect the price of a custom job.
cta: Want an estimate for your job?
contact: Send approximate measurements, photos and a description of what you need. We’ll discuss the details and explain what the initial estimate covers.
content:
“How much per metre?” is a sensible starting question for some metalwork. It gives you a way to judge whether a project might fit your budget. But a length on its own rarely describes the full job.

A plain worktop and one with cupboards and several sinks can have the same overall dimensions while involving different materials and work. At Midia M Metal, we explain the estimate around the item you actually need.

Material and quantity

The type of metal and the amount required are part of the price. Thickness and construction need to suit the intended use, so we discuss those details alongside dimensions.

Tell us if you need several matching pieces. Preparing a set of identical brackets is a different job from making several brackets with individual shapes and fixing positions. We need the quantity and any differences to quote accurately.

Shape and fabrication work

Cutting, forming, welding and finishing contribute to the work involved. Openings, bends, connections and access panels can make two similar-looking items quite different to produce.

A photo explains appearance, but it may not show the construction underneath. A sketch and a description of how the item will be used help us identify the details that affect the job.

Layout and finish

For kitchen units, sink positions, cupboard arrangements and the space for existing equipment all matter. For a frame or enclosure, the mounting arrangement and access requirements can be just as important.

Tell us which surfaces will be visible and what finish you expect. If the new piece needs to match existing metalwork, include clear photographs. We will agree the finish within the quoted scope.

Delivery and installation

A finished item may need delivery only, or it may need fitting on site. Size, access and location affect how that work is arranged.

Include your postcode and mention stairs, narrow entrances, restricted working hours or old equipment that affects access. We confirm the agreed scope of delivery and installation rather than assume those details are included.

Why an estimate can change

Our initial estimate is based on the information available. Exact measurements and design choices can change the final price in either direction.

For example, a customer may initially describe a four-metre cupboard unit, then choose a layout with sink sections and different storage. The final measured length and construction may be different from the original enquiry.

Preparing a quote is free. Site measurement is usually free, depending on location, and any charge is confirmed beforehand. We present the final price and agreed details for your approval before production starts.

How to compare quotes usefully

Check that each quote covers the same dimensions, material, finish, fittings and installation work. Ask whether the amount is an estimate or a final price and what is included in the total.

If you have a budget, tell us early. We can discuss your priorities and suitable options. For a simple enquiry checklist, see what to send for a custom metalwork quote.

title: Commercial Kitchen Canopies and Ductwork: Planning Around Your Space
excerpt: Planning a kitchen canopy or ductwork change? Start with the cooking equipment, available route and site details before agreeing the fabrication.
contact: Send photos of the cooking line, existing canopy and visible duct route, along with your postcode. Tell us what equipment or layout is changing.
content:
A new canopy needs to work with the cooking equipment and the route available for the ductwork. Measuring the wall above the cooking line gives us a starting point, but it does not describe the whole ventilation job.

At Midia M Metal, we make kitchen canopies and ductwork to agreed requirements. We also discuss changes to existing installations. Good information about the equipment and site helps us establish what the work needs to include.

Start with the cooking equipment

Tell us what appliances sit beneath the proposed canopy and provide model details or specifications where available. Explain whether the cooking line is staying as it is or whether you are adding or moving equipment.

Different layouts and uses need assessment. We do not choose the full arrangement from canopy width alone. The equipment information and site requirements need to be considered before the job is agreed.

Show the available duct route

Send wide photographs of the kitchen and any visible existing ductwork. Include the ceiling area, changes in direction and the proposed destination where known.

Mention other services, limited ceiling space and areas that are difficult to access. If there are drawings or an existing ventilation specification, send those too. We can identify what needs further checking during the planning stage.

Existing systems need context

If you are replacing only a canopy or one section of ductwork, explain why. Is the kitchen layout changing, is a component damaged, or has the existing arrangement become unsuitable?

A replacement component has to be considered as part of the installation around it. Photographs and dimensions help with the initial discussion, but further inspection may be needed before we can confirm the appropriate work.

Plan for access after installation

The arrangement should be discussed with cleaning, inspection and maintenance access in mind. Tell us about areas that are currently difficult to reach and any restrictions around the proposed route.

Also provide any project requirements or approvals that have already been identified. We agree the fabrication and installation scope alongside the relevant site information; a custom-made canopy alone does not establish that the complete system meets every requirement.

Agree timing around the kitchen

Let us know whether the premises are being fitted out or already operating. Working hours, delivery access and the availability of the cooking area affect how installation can be arranged.

Once the equipment details, dimensions, scope and price are agreed, we can provide an estimated production and installation schedule. Timing depends on the job and our workload.

What to send for the first conversation

  • Photos of the cooking equipment and surrounding kitchen.
  • Approximate canopy dimensions and ceiling height.
  • Equipment specifications and existing drawings, if available.
  • Photos of the visible duct route.
  • A description of the proposed changes and your postcode.

If the kitchen also needs new units, our guide to made-to-measure worktops explains how we plan their layout and measurements.

title: What to Send Us for a Custom Metalwork Quote
excerpt: You do not need a finished drawing to ask for a metalwork quote. Start with photos, rough measurements, the intended use and your postcode.
cta: Ready to talk through the job?
contact: Send the details you have. A few photos, approximate measurements and your postcode are enough to begin the conversation.
content:
You don’t need to draw a perfect plan before calling a metal fabricator. Often, a few clear photos and an explanation of what you need are enough to start a useful conversation.

At Midia M Metal, we prepare free quotes for bespoke metalwork and discuss the details with you before production. Sending the information below helps us understand the job and identify anything that needs checking.

Explain what you want the piece to do

Start with the problem. Perhaps a ready-made cupboard will not fit, a replacement bracket is unavailable, or you need a cover that can be removed for maintenance.

You can describe it in ordinary language. Tell us what matters most: usable storage, a particular appearance, matching existing equipment or making better use of an awkward space.

Take a wide photo as well as a close-up

A close-up shows the detail. A wider photo shows where it belongs and what surrounds it. For a repair, include the damaged area and the complete item. For a new unit, show the space from more than one angle.

Photograph nearby doors, pipework and equipment where they affect the fit. If there is an existing piece to match, show its connections as well as its front.

Add approximate measurements

Length, width and height are a useful start. A rough sketch with labelled dimensions is often easier to follow than several numbers in a message. Use one unit consistently and mark anything you have estimated.

For a replacement part, fixing positions may be important too. You do not need to establish every production dimension yourself; tell us what you know and we will explain what else is needed.

Include the use, material and quantity

Tell us what the item supports, contains or connects to, and where it will be used. Mention outdoor exposure, cleaning requirements or regular movement where relevant.

If you have a required material or specification, send it. Otherwise, we can discuss a suitable choice. Include the quantity, particularly if you need a set of matching pieces or slightly different versions.

Tell us where and when

Your postcode helps us discuss delivery and any site work. Mention stairs, narrow entrances, restricted access and whether the premises will remain in use during installation.

If you have a target date, include it from the start. We will discuss the available timing for the job rather than assume a fixed turnaround.

What happens after you enquire?

We talk through the requirements and prepare an initial estimate from the information available. If that is acceptable, we arrange the next steps, including a site visit where needed.

Site measurement is usually free, depending on location, and any charge is confirmed beforehand. We then agree the final measurements, design, price and scope of work with you. Production starts after your approval.

The metalwork pricing guide explains why the final price may differ from an early estimate. For examples of the items we make, see our bespoke fabrication guide.
